title: Machine Learning Prediction of Photovoltaic Power Output from Environmental Variables
abstract: The accurate prediction of photovoltaic (PV) power output enables the reliable integration of solar power into electricity grids, but the comparisons of machine learning models published in the literature often differ in the method of handling data, the method of validation, and the extent to which the models are interpretable. Authors developed a simple and repeatable computational framework that uses solar energy data from a real and publicly available hourly dataset of around 8,000 observations, including solar irradiance, temperature, humidity, wind speed, and PV power output, to predict PV power output from environmental data. Preprocessing of the data, treatment of missing values and engineering of the temporal and lagged features were done prior to splitting the data in chronological order into a training (70 %), a validation (15 %), and a testing subset (15 %). Random Forest Regression, Support Vector Regression and XGBoost were implemented in Python, and their hyperparameters were optimized by using Bayesian search and expanding-window time-series cross validation during the training process. The untouched test subset was used to assess the predictive performance of the models and to determine the most influential environmental variables, using the mean absolute error (MAE), the root mean square error (RMSE) and the coefficient of determination (R²) metrics, and applying Shapley additive explanations (SHAP). Reproducibility was facilitated by fixed random seeds, version controlled code, recorded software environment and documented data lineage.

title: An Edge Device for Real-Time Fake and Tampered Audio Detection
abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence enables realistic speech generation through text-to-speech, voice cloning, and speech synthesis, which can also be misused for impersonation, fraud, and misinformation.This paper presents "An Edge Device for Real-Time Fake and Tampered Audio Detection," a software-based system that uses Digital Signal Processing (DSP) techniques to analyze audio authenticity.The input audio is divided into short frames, and features such as Zero Crossing Rate (ZCR) variance, Auto-Correlation (AC) variance, and Root Mean Square (RMS) variance are extracted to capture variations in phonetic activity, pitch periodicity, and amplitude dynamics.A mathematical scoring and decision mechanism combines these features to estimate whether an audio signal is AI-generated or manipulated.The system aims to provide a lightweight and responsive solution for real-time audio authenticity analysis while considering challenges such as noise, compression, and recording conditions.

title: Reproducibility archive for An Information-Centered Audit of Retraining-Free Adaptation in Liquid and Recurrent Networks
abstract: This code-and-data reproducibility archive supports the study "An Information-Centered Audit of Retraining-Free Adaptation in Liquid and Recurrent Networks" by Yifei Long. It provides an information-centered audit of concept-drift adaptation in liquid and recurrent networks, including frozen protocols and configurations, preparation/training/analysis code, seed-level and lower-level outputs, editable figures and their source data, and SHA-256 integrity checks. All 80 formal and 12 separate validation checkpoints from the causal-feedback extension are included. Earlier primary trained checkpoints were not retained: the archived metrics support reanalysis, while additional predictions require rerunning the recorded training workflows. No clean-machine end-to-end reproduction or cross-platform bitwise identity is claimed. The manuscript text, submission correspondence, author photograph and private conversations are excluded. Third-party raw datasets are not redistributed; access/preparation scripts and provenance are provided. AI-assistance provenance is documented without disclosing private conversations. title: Research on the construction of alpine mountain areas meteorological support knowledge graph based on large language model
authors: Gu Shuanglong, Shi Xiaomin, Tu Yiqiang, Lu Kui, Wang Guoshun
abstract: There are problems including vague text semantics, fragmented information and insufficient domain adaptability in the field of alpine mountain areas meteorological support, which restrict the capabilities of intelligent semantic modeling and decision support. Against this background, this paper proposes ChatGLM-AMKG, a knowledge graph construction method for alpine mountain areas meteorological support based on the ChatGLM3-6B large language model. This method aims to improve the accuracy and generalization ability of domain knowledge extraction and facilitate the development of intelligent semantic modeling for alpine mountain areas meteorological support. Firstly, a knowledge representation schema covering core categories such as geographical environment, meteorological elements and military operations is established in combination with domain characteristics. Secondly, a step-by-step prompting strategy integrating Few-shot examples, Chain-of-Thought reasoning and constraint prompts is designed to guide ChatGLM3-6B to realize high-quality triple extraction from multi-source heterogeneous domain data with only a small amount of manual annotation. Subsequently, a structured knowledge graph is constructed via knowledge fusion and visual management. Finally, comparative experiments and ablation experiments are conducted to verify the effectiveness of the proposed method. Experimental results demonstrate that the F1-score of ChatGLM-AMKG reaches 91.1% and 87.6% in entity recognition and relation extraction respectively, which are increased by 12.2% and 13.5% compared with general models. In contrast with the average performance after removing the step-by-step prompting strategy, its F1-score is improved by 8.9% and 9.8% in the above two tasks correspondingly. ChatGLM-AMKG exhibits favorable scalability in application scenarios such as meteorological semantic retrieval and decision support, and provides a reproducible and popularizable technical approach for the intelligent development of alpine mountain areas meteorological support.

title: Проблемы применения искусственного интеллекта в патентном праве
abstract: Статья посвящена комплексному анализу проблем, возникающих в сфере патентного права в связи с активным развитием технологий искусственного интеллекта (ИИ). В условиях стремительного роста числа патентных заявок, связанных с ИИ, в работе, с опорой на отечественное законодательство и мировой опыт (включая прецедент системы DABUS), рассматриваются ключевые вызовы: отсутствие у ИИ правосубъектности; сложности определения авторства и распределения прав между разработчиком, оператором и пользователем нейросетей по модели коллективного авторства, а также проблемы адекватной оценки критерия «изобретательского уровня» для решений, сгенерированных алгоритмами. Также поднимаются вопросы деликтоспособности и ответственности за автономное нарушение патентных прав, в том числе обсуждается концепция обязательного страхования таких рисков. Отмечается двойственная роль ИИ, выступающего не только генератором объектов интеллектуальной собственности, но и инструментом их защиты, что сопровождается рисками алгоритмической предвзятости и ложных срабатываний. На основе анализа научной доктрины автор приходит к выводу о необходимости формирования сбалансированного, технологически нейтрального специального правового режима, закрепляющего права за человеком. Это позволит сохранить баланс между стимулированием инноваций и защитой базовых принципов патентной системы в цифровую эпоху.

title: Artificial intelligence and digital health in bronchoscopy: advances in diagnostic accuracy, real-time navigation and procedural skills training
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and procedure-linked digital health technologies are beginning to transform bronchoscopy across three interconnected domains. In terms of diagnostic accuracy, deep learning models applied to endobronchial ultrasound images and bronchoscopic videos can match or exceed human readers in differentiating benign from malignant lesions, although nearly all evidence remains at the level of test-accuracy metrics rather than clinical outcomes. In real-time navigation, AI-augmented fluoroscopy and tomosynthesis platforms represent the clearest example of clinically deployed AI that improves lesion localisation and diagnostic yield for peripheral pulmonary nodules, while camera-based localisation and shared-control robotic systems remain largely preclinical. In training, multiple randomised controlled trials demonstrate that AI-guided simulators significantly improve performance across experience levels, and that AI-derived metrics can objectively assess competence, although the first attempt to show impact on real-world clinical performance was inconclusive. This review synthesises the current literature across these three domains, distinguishing technologies that are currently used in clinical practice with supportive published evidence from those that remain investigational. It provides practising bronchoscopists and trainees with a balanced appraisal of what AI can realistically offer today, what limitations persist, and what developments are likely over the coming decade.

title: A dynamical systems approach for stabilization of spin-12 quantum systems under continuous measurement
abstract: We propose a novel dynamic feedback control strategy for stabilizing two-level quantum systems undergoing continuous quantum non-demolition measurements. The control input is constructed via the gradient of a quadratic cost functional, enabling systematic convergence towards the target eigenstate of the measurement operator. The resulting closed-loop system exhibits exponential convergence, where the stochastic measurement-induced diffusion acts constructively in the stabilization process. Notably, the controller requires only the measurement-axis projection of the quantum state, motivating a reduced-order filtering structure. Numerical simulations on a spin- 1 2 system validate the theoretical guarantees. The design framework is structurally simple and, hence, can be scaled to higher-dimensional quantum systems.

title: GPT-assisted formative feedback for middle-school linear function inquiry: Design and classroom evaluation of a gamified AlgeoMath module
abstract: Objective This study examined how GPT-assisted formative feedback could be integrated into classroom inquiry on linear functions. Methods A gamified AlgeoMath module combined rule-based graph checks, staged language-model hints, and rubric-based reports. The pilot involved 49 students in two convenience-sampled intact middle school classes. Analyses integrated submission logs, module scores, immediate pre-post surveys, expert review, and human-AI agreement. Results Task completion was near complete. Among initially incorrect task instances followed by a second submission, 57.5% were corrected on that submission. Module profiles highlighted covariation and mathematical justification as areas needing further support. Six of eight survey items increased after Holm correction in 48 matched pairs. Expert review primarily identified mismatches between feedback content and its intended scaffold level. Automated rubric categories agreed with each of two educators on 69% of 100 sampled responses. Conclusions The study connects classroom implementation with evidence about students' response patterns and feedback quality. It identifies scaffold calibration and the interpretation of partial reasoning as priorities for teacher-supervised AI feedback in linear function inquiry and provides a basis for evaluating learning outcomes in subsequent controlled studies.

title: Least Squares for Time Series Forecasting
abstract: A time-series forecast is scored on a future value of the series. A representation loss that regresses the next latent, as in LeNEPA, is a different least-squares problem on the same bottleneck. We write both programs down. The forecast program minimizes the error of a decoded latent on the coordinate that will be reported. For a scalar target and a linear decoder, every latent rank of at least one matches ordinary least squares, and an isotropy constraint is only a rescaling: after the decoder is refit, the forecast does not move. The other program fits the whole next vector at a fixed rank, then freezes the encoder and attaches a head. On a four-dimensional series whose last three coordinates are the same autoregression, that rank-1 fit puts mass $0.9998$ on the repeated coordinate and forecasts the remaining signal at the marginal variance $2.794$. The forecast program puts mass $1$ on the signal and matches the innovation variance $0.992$. Rank $2$ gives the vector fit a second direction, and the two programs agree. Iterating the fitted one-step coefficient $0.803$ raises the open-loop error from $0.992$ at one step to $2.700$ at eight steps.

title: FFBL-Coop: Association-Decoupled Cooperative 3D Multi-Object Tracking
abstract: Cooperative 3D tracking must integrate complementary observations across agents and time while maintaining consistent identities. When evidence integration and identity inheritance share a matching decision, errors arising from cross-view appearance differences and spatial misalignment can compromise both feature fusion and track continuity. We propose FFBL-Coop, a fuse first, bind later framework that separates instance admission from identity management. Confidence-ranked Slot Admission (CSA) allocates cooperative queries to available ego slots using confidence and spatial proximity. Unified Representation Aggregation (URA) uses cooperative semantic features and aligned anchors to guide ego-feature retrieval, refining the augmented query bank within a shared transformer decoder. After refinement, Cooperative-Priority Identity Anchoring (CPIA) combines learned association with persistent mappings to establish accepted identity assignments across frames. A shared codebook reduces transmitted payload while retaining AP and AMOTA close to the uncompressed variant. FFBL-Coop achieves AMOTA/AP of 0.611/0.548 on V2X-Seq and 0.688/0.653 on Griffin-25M. Code will be released.

title: PyCDFT: A Python-scriptable library for analytical evaluation of orbital conceptual density (matrix) functional theory
abstract: Conceptual density functional theory (CDFT) defines chemical reactivity descriptors as derivatives of the electronic energy with respect to the number of electrons and the external potential, or combinations thereof; in practice, however, researchers almost always replace these derivatives with finite-difference and frontier-orbital approximations, and no common software exists for their analytical evaluation. We present PyCDFT, to our knowledge, the first standardized, open-source, and scriptable code that analytically computes the descriptors of conceptual density (matrix) functional theory for ground and excited states up to second order, including the orbital hardness, the Fukui function and Fukui matrix, and the linear response function, from a single converged mean-field wavefunction imported from virtually any electronic-structure package. The descriptors are obtained from matrix-free, preconditioned Krylov-subspace solutions of the coupled-perturbed self-consistent-field equations for both spin-unpolarized and spin-polarized references, with the work distributed over MPI ranks and all data flowing through a single HDF5 checkpoint file that supports restart, post-processing, and the export of real-space descriptors as cube files for visualization. The design delegates integrals, grids, and exchange-correlation kernels to PySCF and Libxc, keeping the library compact, user-friendly, and interoperable. Worked examples on the ground state of H_2O and a broken-symmetry ΔSCF excited state of NH_3 show that a complete second-order CDFT analysis requires only a few lines of user code.

title: LawCompass: Navigating from Legal QA to Multi-Agent Deep Research with Grounded Evidence
abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) have significantly democratized access to legal information. Nevertheless, most existing legal assistants remain confined to multi-turn conversational QA, failing to support complex legal tasks that require systematic evidence retrieval, multi-step reasoning, and report-level synthesis. In this paper, we present LawCompass, an evidence-grounded legal assistant that navigates the transition from standard Legal QA to multi-agent deep research. LawCompass provides three task-oriented functions: Legal QA, which delivers precise, evidence-backed answers to legal questions; Professional Retrieval, which enables structured exploration of statutes and judicial cases via query rewriting; and Deep Research, which employs a multi-agent workflow to decompose complex legal tasks and synthesize comprehensive research reports. Crucially, LawCompass maintains explicit citation links across all modules, empowering users to directly verify system outputs against original legal sources. Evaluation results demonstrate that LawCompass provides a practical and scalable paradigm for transforming conversational AI into trustworthy and evidence-grounded legal research assistance.

title: Full-Domain Coupler: A Wireless Native Neural Backbone for Channel Representation and Deduction
abstract: Data representation is a fundamental issue in deep learning. However, as wireless data scale and deeply couple across many physical domains such as time, space, and frequency, existing wireless artificial intelligence (AI) technologies lack dedicated representation solutions. Instead, they mainly rely on stitching general-purpose networks, a “tool-driven” paradigm that inevitably results in structural redundancy and bottlenecks in information flow. To fill this gap, this paper proposes Coupler, a wireless native-AI neural backbone designed for the representation learning of channel state information—the pivotal data in wireless systems. Leveraging the physical insights revealed by channel tensors, Coupler decomposes representation learning into individual domains on a layer-by-layer basis and then couples the learned domain-specific features through a dimension-staggered cascade. This full-domain interleaved learning architecture enables superior parameter efficiency and fine-grained multi-domain feature fusion. Based on this backbone, we use complex-domain multilayer perceptrons as spatial and frequency domain learners, while employing three optional mechanisms—convolution, attention, or gating—to capture temporal dependencies. This results in a series of efficient and extremely lightweight channel learning schemes with diverse functionalities, showcasing the compactness, versatility, and flexibility of Coupler. We evaluate these schemes on channel deduction, a general representation task encompassing channel estimation, interpolation, prediction, and feedback. Extensive experimental evaluations validate the significant performance gains and robust applicability, even for real-world measured data, demonstrating Coupler’s potential as a promising basic architecture in the design of wireless foundation models.

title: Monotone and Nonmonotone Linearized Block Coordinate Descent Methods for Nonsmooth Composite Optimization Problems
abstract: Abstract In this paper, we introduce both monotone and nonmonotone variants of LiBCoD, a Li nearized B lock Co ordinate D escent method for solving composite optimization problems. At each iteration, a random block is selected, and the smooth components of the objective are linearized along the chosen block in a Gauss-Newton approach. For the monotone variant, we establish a global sublinear convergence rate to a stationary point under the assumption of bounded iterates. For the nonmonotone variant, we derive a global sublinear convergence rate without requiring global Lipschitz continuity or bounded iterates. Preliminary numerical experiments highlight the promising performance of the proposed approach.

title: Benchmark-Normalized Systematic Literature Review of Attribute-Based Encryption Overhead in Blockchain-Based Cloud Data Management
abstract: Systematic literature reviews on Attribute-Based Encryption (ABE) for blockchain-based cloud data management typically present qualitative comparisons disregarding hardware, cryptographic library, security level, policy depth, and consensus settings, so reported overheads remain incomparable across studies. We propose a Benchmark-Normalized SLR Framework reconfiguring the ABE module of a permissioned blockchain-based cloud data management system as a benchmark-aware, overhead-classified, and evidence-normalized subsystem instead of a monolithic cryptographic black box. The framework expands the conventional ABE module by means of three components: a Benchmark Normalization Kernel that maps raw time and communication measurements from thirty primary studies into a dimensionless, cross-platform comparable space via reference-hardware scaling and communication normalization; an Overhead Pattern Classifier that applies Ward-linkage agglomerative clustering with silhouette-score-based dendrogram cutting and decision-rule refinement to assign each scheme to one of four overhead classes, comprising pairing-bound, policy-size-bound, revocation-heavy, and communication-efficient; and a PRISMA-Guided Evidence Synthesizer that orchestrates the review protocol and produces a structured evidence base linking normalized costs to security assumptions, revocation methods, and deployment suitability. These components interchange structured data with the key generation authority, ciphertext policy engine, and revocation mechanism via a feedback loop selecting the ABE scheme minimizing normalized overhead subject to security, revocation, and deployment constraints. The framework consequently yields a reproducible, quantitative, and cross-platform comparable taxonomy of ABE schemes, and it permits designers of blockchain-cloud stacks to make evidence-based scheme selections rather than depending on incomparable, platform-specific measurements.

title: Semantic Interface Model v1.0 for MUSE 2.0 and TCR 3.0: A classical information-theoretic and information-geometric framework for 'meaning', with exact toy models and worked Fisher-geometry examples
abstract: This paper sets out the Semantic Interface Model, the classical core under two layers of the Möbius Project: MUSE 2.0, a quantitative reading of "meaning-bearing flow", and TCR 3.0, which keeps from the Theory of Cognitive Relativity the idea that geometry is relative to the observer and defines that geometry, for regular interpreters, as the Fisher geometry of their parameter spaces. A perceptual or communicative channel is modeled as a Markov chain Y → S → X → Z from a task variable Y through a physical state S and a sensor signal X to an internal representation Z. Its semantic energy is E_sem := I(Y; Z), Shannon mutual information in bits or nats. Nothing in this is new physics, and the quantity itself is not new: in the information-bottleneck literature it is the relevant information a representation keeps about a target. Three layers are built on it. The scalar semantic aperture is the information an interpreter's output retains about the task, divided by a reference value; with the interface's own semantic energy as the reference, it is the fraction retained. It lies in [0, 1] under the two normalizations recommended here and can exceed 1 under a third, which is flagged. The tensorial aperture is a task-weighted Fisher information metric on the interpreter's parameter space. It measures how sensitive the interpreter's predictions are to its parameters, not how much semantic energy it uses, and no inequality links it to the scalar form. Cognitive curvature, the term by which TCR 3.0 meets information geometry, is the curvature of the Levi-Civita connection of that metric — not the metric itself, which the 2025 draft conflated with curvature. Worked examples make this concrete. A Gaussian location-scale interpreter, and a linear-Gaussian interpreter reading any representation with finite, nonzero second moment, both have constant curvature −1/2, the classical curvature of the normal family; a two-parameter logistic interpreter is flat when the representation takes two values and, at a computed point, curved when it takes three; and a categorical interpreter over three outcomes has constant positive curvature +1/4 even though it ignores the representation. Curvature in this sense is a property of an interpreter reading a representation, not of the true relation between task and representation, and not of meaning at large. The paper also gives exact semantic energies for two toy interfaces, a growth hypothesis relating semantic energy to physical power and the conditions under which it is testable, a CMOS imaging interface as the device example, and a map of where these definitions sit in the published line. A script checks the worked examples, the toy-channel values and the aperture bounds, the last by a randomized property test. No theorem here is new, and no measurement on a deployed system is reported. The verification script (Appendix A, AGPL-3.0-or-later) needs Python 3 and SymPy and checks the worked examples, the toy-channel values and the aperture bounds; it exits non-zero if any check fails. The September 2026 revision (corrections, worked examples, verification script, positioning and prose) was generated by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic) under the author's direction. Its successive drafts were checked in four rounds of adversarial refutation, each round covering mathematics, consistency and scope: eleven passes in all, because the fourth round combined mathematics and consistency in one pass. Each pass was run by a separate Claude Opus 5.5 agent with its own context — the same model that generated the revision. The fourth-round draft was also given an editorial read for internal contradictions by a model of a different family, OpenAI's gpt-5.6-sol run through the Codex CLI; all eleven of its items, eight marked must-fix, were checked against the text and corrected. A fifth round, a single confirmation pass by a separate Claude Opus 5.5 agent, checked the edits made in response to the fourth round and the editorial read. A sixth round, another single confirmation pass by a separate Claude Opus 5.5 agent, checked the corrections the fifth round prompted and a positive-curvature example added afterwards; the corrections it prompted were not themselves re-reviewed. The verification script was re-run on the final text. No human referee has reviewed the text. The author reviewed the deposited text and takes responsibility for it. title: Haruco: A New Russian-Language Corpus of Popular Science Texts with Coreference Annotation
abstract: Abstract— This paper presents a new Russian-language corpus with coreference annotation, HaRuCo (Habr Russian Coreference Corpus). The corpus is based on popular science articles related to the subject area of Computational Linguistics. The paper proposes a method for coreference annotation in texts from narrow subject areas, which includes four main stages: syntactic analysis of the text, assembly of noun phrases and identification of pronouns for constructing mentions (spans), classification of mentions by subject area classes, and clustering of mentions according to chains of coreferentially linked spans. Coreferential links were annotated using a syntactic parser and a large language model, followed by manual verification and correction. The created corpus includes 3727 entities, 9905 mentions, and 2683 coreferential chains. The created corpus can be used for training and evaluating coreference resolution models for the Russian language.

title: JevSpec: Training-Free, Auditable Typed Decision Specs for Budgeted Feature Acquisition
abstract: Structured decision models that return typed outputs, such as choices, judgments, and scores, enable efficient decisions but often leave the evidence behind each call unauditable. title: Evaluation of In-Corpus SimCLR Pretraining for Underwater Acoustic Target Recognition Under Recording-Disjoint Splits
abstract: Label scarcity limits underwater acoustic target recognition (UATR) and motivates self-supervised learning on large unlabeled hydrophone archives, yet the benefit is unclear when training and test recordings may not overlap. This controlled pilot evaluates in-corpus SimCLR pretraining on 176,481 unlabeled log-mel clips pooled from the training partitions of Oceanship, QiandaoEar22, and a reconstructed VTUAD corpus. A ResNet-18 encoder is evaluated on each corpus under recording-/clip-disjoint splits with linear probing and full fine-tuning against ImageNet and random initialization. Under linear probing, SimCLR trails ImageNet features on VTUAD (accuracy −0.0829, paired p = 0.017) and QiandaoEar22 (−0.0533, p = 0.012), with only a non-significant edge on Oceanship; after fine-tuning, gaps are small and SimCLR is nominally worse on VTUAD accuracy (−0.0388, p = 0.034). VTUAD probes show a stable validation–test gap and higher training-recording separability than both controls; normalization controls leave this intact. The main analysis covers 45 downstream configurations on one encoder; robustness checks add two encoders, corpus balancing, and checkpoint-rule variants. Extending pretraining to 100–200 epochs does not close the gap, channel-varying augmentation halves it, and a VICReg objective reproduces it (Section 4.4). Across seeds 42/43/44, cross-encoder standard deviation of downstream test accuracy is 0.002–0.009; both probe-accuracy deficits replicate in the same direction on all three encoders (p ≤ 0.017). These observations are consistent with recording-specific information in the learned features, but do not establish that it causes the deficits. We derive design requirements for future UATR evaluation: cross-site pretraining, channel-varying augmentation, balanced corpus sampling, and recording-identity controls.

title: An intelligent artificial intelligence framework for business insight generation from streaming data
abstract: Big data analytics helps organizations leverage their data to uncover new opportunities, leading to smarter decisions, more efficient operations, and ultimately higher profits. Effective use of big data and creating important predictive models make it more straightforward for a business to realize what the consumer likes and what he or she does not. This will enable the business to propose better offers and administrations with their items when contrasted to its competitors. In this paper, the authors suggest the use of a big data analytics platform combined with natural language processing (NLP) techniques to do the intelligent processing of unstructured streaming data. A new method utilizing Apache Spark pipelining is proposed to achieve predictive analytics for unstructured data streams. With this predictive model, mining of the unstructured streaming data can be done and intelligent predictions are made possible in real time using artificial intelligence techniques.

title: B-254 A Self-Cleaning Dual-Architecture Approach for Detecting Random Errors in Clinical Laboratory Reaction Course Data with Limited Training Samples
abstract: Abstract Background Clinical laboratories rely heavily on Internal Quality Control (IQC) to detect systemic errors such as reagent degradation or calibration shifts. However, IQC is intermittent and often powerless against random errors affecting individual patient samples (e.g., fibrin clots, micro-bubbles, or drug interference). Reaction course data, which captures the entire chemical kinetic process, contains rich information for identifying these anomalies but remains underutilized due to the complexity of analyzing time-series data without massive labeled datasets. We developed an unsupervised, self-cleaning dual-architecture system designed to serve as a continuous "Safety Net" for detecting both known and unknown random errors in routine clinical chemistry data, overcoming the "Big Data" barrier for individual laboratories. Methods This study utilized routine clinical chemistry data (N=1,995; Copper assay) collected over six months from a single facility. The proposed system employs a Dual-Architecture Framework designed to detect anomalies through two complementary mechanisms. Phase 1 uses a deep Autoencoder with specialized 1D layers to learn the latent representation of normal reaction kinetics and flags waveform distortions based on reconstruction error. Phase 2 employs a pretrained deep convolutional neural network (CNN) to extract visual features from converted reaction curve images, using an isolation-based algorithm for anomaly detection. To handle noisy real-world data, we implemented an Iterative Refinement (Self-Cleaning) strategy. Samples exceeding a dynamic anomaly threshold were identified as candidates, and a simplified density-based filter was applied to distinguish truly unique anomalous patterns from random statistical noise. This allowed the model to autonomously purify its training set using only unlabeled historical data. Results The Autoencoder initially flagged a substantial portion of the data (18.2%) as potential candidates, a rate consistent with the noise inherent in raw clinical data. The subsequent CNN-based visual verification refined this pool, identifying 40 potential anomalies. Crucially, strictly "Dual Verified" anomalies (confirmed by both models) were reduced to just 0.05% of the total samples. This tiny fraction included a specific anomaly missed by standard rule-based checks (limit and linearity checks) but successfully identified by our system. Visual analysis revealed a non-monotonic deviation in the reaction curve caused by M-protein induced turbidity. The self-cleaning process significantly improved model discrimination, achieving a Separation Ratio (mean MSE of anomalies / mean MSE of normals) of >400 for the Main wavelength and >650 for the Sub wavelength. Robustness analysis with varying sample sizes (N=200 to 1,995) demonstrated that the anomaly separation capability plateaus around N=1,000, indicating that a single laboratory's accumulated data is sufficient for stable training. The entire training process was completed in approximately 25 minutes on a standard PC. Conclusion This study demonstrates that an unsupervised, self-cleaning dual-architecture system can effectively detect subtle, unknown random errors that bypass traditional IQC. By leveraging iterative self-cleaning learning, high-precision anomaly detection is achievable with limited training samples from a single center. This approach provides a practical, scalable pathway for the democratization of AI in routine laboratories, transforming reaction data from a passive archive into an active quality assurance tool.

title: TREMOR: Template Matching for Large Seismic Data Collections
abstract: Seismic station networks continuously record the ground velocity at several locations on earth in the form of waveform data series, which seismologists analyze to detect various kinds of geophysical events, including earthquakes. Some of these events are of particular interest: they are called templates and are used to search the seismic data collections for matching, similar events. This is known as template matching, and is a fundamental task in seismology, serving as the backbone for various seismic analyses. However, template matching requires extensive processing times, especially for seismic collections that exceed the memory capacity of a single machine. This poses a significant challenge to seismologists and is becoming worse as the seismological datasets continue to grow in size. In this paper, we introduce TREMOR, a distributed data series processing framework for template matching, designed to efficiently handle large waveform collections. We apply TREMOR to two representative real-world seismic use cases for template matching and, through an extensive experimental evaluation, we demonstrate its efficiency, with TREMOR being up to 12x faster than the best competing method, while returning the same, exact results.

title: Slow-Fast Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for Capability Preservation
abstract: Foundation multimodal large language models are designed to support a broad spectrum of capabilities across diverse domains. Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) provides an effective framework for consolidating domain-specific expertise into a single student model. However, MOPD training gradually drives the student away from its initialization model, and general capabilities decline as the displacement grows, resulting in capability interference. A direct remedy is constraining the student toward its initialization, but this suppresses the acquisition of domain expertise as well. We propose Slow-Fast Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (SF-MOPD), which couples a fast model, the current student updated directly by each teacher, with a slow model, an exponential moving average of the student. The slow model absorbs the learning signal gradually, serving as a moving capability reference that fuses the general foundation with confirmed domain expertise. For each teacher, SF-MOPD computes the teacher-induced update in log-probability space and removes only the component that pushes the fast model further away from the slow model, while retaining aligned and orthogonal components. Experiments across multiple model scales demonstrate that SF-MOPD effectively mitigates capability interference, enhances specialized multimodal capabilities, and reduces the average degradation on general-capability benchmarks, consistently outperforming vanilla MOPD.

title: Designing for Interpretation Uncertainty: Architecture and Principles for Topological Learning Analytics Dashboards
abstract: Topological Data Analysis (TDA) offers novel methods for understanding temporal dynamics in complex systems, yet its application in information systems design faces a fundamental challenge: how should systems present analytical outputs when interpretation frameworks are still developing? This paper reports on the development of TopoLA, a dashboard system applying Zigzag Persistent Homology to learning management system data, and proposes three early design principles for interpretation support in emerging analytics: (1) separation of objective measurement from contextual interpretation, (2) graduated disclosure from metrics through patterns to reflective prompts, and (3) explicit acknowledgment of methodological uncertainty. The system implements a modular three-stage pipeline--feature extraction, topological computation, and interpretation support--enabling extension to additional analytical methods. This work contributes to information systems research by articulating preliminary design knowledge for systems that must communicate analytical insights from methods lacking established interpretation norms--a challenge increasingly common as novel computational techniques enter applied domains.

title: Nonlinear stability of the Guderley imploding shock wave in radial symmetry
abstract: We prove nonlinear stability of the Guderley imploding shock under radial perturbations for the three-dimensional compressible Euler equations in the adiabatic range 1<γleq5{3}. The perturbed solutions develop an asymptotically self-similar implosion in finite time. Our result allows perturbations with small, nonzero constant pressure in the quiescent region ahead of the shock. The proof combines weighted L^infty estimates along characteristics with a computer-assisted proof of stability inequalities for the Guderley profile.
